# The universal property of a theory generated by a pair of subobjects

The construction answers two questions. Given an assignment of generators, does it extend uniquely to a translation? Given the translation, when does it preserve the theory generated by positive and negative axioms? The free presentation gives the unique translation. The least theory containing the specified axioms determines when this translation preserves the theory.

## 1. Generators relative to a functor

Let $S:\mathcal P\to\mathcal C$ be a functor and let $X$ be an object of $\mathcal C$. A **free presentation on $X$** consists of an object $P_X$ of $\mathcal P$ and a morphism $\eta_X:X\to S(P_X)$ such that for every $Q$ in $\mathcal P$ the map

$$
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal P}(P_X,Q)
\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,S(Q)),
\qquad \sigma\longmapsto S(\sigma)\eta_X
$$

is a bijection. Write $\widehat f:P_X\to Q$ for the unique morphism corresponding to $f:X\to S(Q)$. The bijection is natural in $Q$ by composition. Free presentations chosen for every $X$ give a left adjoint $F$ to $S$, with $FX=P_X$.

The universal property specifies how $X$ generates $P_X$. The unit can fail to be monic. For instance, if $S:\mathbf 1\to\mathbf{Set}$ selects a singleton, then $X\to 1$ is universal for every set $X$. The atom constructor for propositional syntax is identified in §4.

## 2. Lifting an adjunction between indexed preorders

Write $\mathbf{Preord}$ for the category of preorders and monotone maps. An **indexed preorder** on $\mathcal C$ is a functor $\mathcal H:\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Preord}$. For $k:X\to Y$, write $k^*:\mathcal H(Y)\to\mathcal H(X)$ for its action. The Grothendieck construction $\int\mathcal H$ has objects $(X,u)$ with $u\in\mathcal H(X)$. A morphism $(X,u)\to(Y,v)$ is a morphism $k:X\to Y$ satisfying $u\le k^*v$. Identities and composition are those of $\mathcal C$. Such a morphism is cartesian precisely when $u$ and $k^*v$ are equivalent in $\mathcal H(X)$, that is, when each is below the other.

**Lifting lemma.** Let $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal P$ be left adjoint to $S:\mathcal P\to\mathcal C$, with unit $\eta$. Let $\mathcal H$ and $\mathcal T$ be indexed preorders on $\mathcal C$ and $\mathcal P$, respectively, and let $\kappa:\mathcal T\Rightarrow \mathcal H\circ S^{\mathrm{op}}$ be natural. It induces the functor $J:\int\mathcal T\to\int\mathcal H$ over $S$ given by $J(Q,t)=(SQ,\kappa_Q(t))$ and $J(\sigma)=S\sigma$.

The adjunction $F\dashv S$ lifts to an adjunction $\Sigma\dashv J$ of the total categories if and only if, for each $X$, the monotone map

$$
M_X=\eta_X^*\kappa_{FX}:\mathcal T(FX)\longrightarrow\mathcal H(X)
$$

has a left adjoint $L_X$. Here a lift has $\Sigma$ over $F$ and its unit and counit over those of $F\dashv S$. Equivalently, for each $u\in\mathcal H(X)$ one can choose a least $t\in\mathcal T(FX)$ with $u\le M_X(t)$. This $t$ is $L_X(u)$, up to equivalence in the preorder. For $A=(X,u)$, the resulting object $((FX,L_X(u)),\eta_X)$ is initial in $A\downarrow J$.

Explicitly, an object of $A\downarrow J$ consists of $(Q,t)$ and $f:X\to SQ$ with $u\le f^*\kappa_Q(t)$. A morphism from $((Q,t),f)$ to $((Q',t'),f')$ is a morphism $\sigma:Q\to Q'$ with $t\le\sigma^*t'$ and $S(\sigma)f=f'$.

**Proof.** For $\sigma:Q\to Q'$, naturality gives $\kappa_Q(\sigma^*t')=(S\sigma)^*\kappa_{Q'}(t')$. Monotonicity of $\kappa_Q$ makes $J$ a functor over $S$. The naturality equation also shows that $J$ preserves cartesian morphisms, since it sends the canonical lift $(Q,\sigma^*t')\to(Q',t')$ to the canonical lift of $S\sigma$ at $J(Q',t')$.

First suppose $L_X\dashv M_X$ for each $X$, and put $\Sigma(X,u)=(FX,L_X(u))$. For $f:X\to SQ$, let $\widehat f:FX\to Q$ be its transpose. The fibre adjunction, naturality of $\kappa$, and $S(\widehat f)\eta_X=f$ give

$$
L_X(u)\le\widehat f^{\,*}t
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
u\le\eta_X^*\kappa_{FX}(\widehat f^{\,*}t)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
u\le f^*\kappa_Q(t).
$$

The defining bound for $L_X(u)$ makes $(\Sigma A,\eta_X)$ an object of $A\downarrow J$. The equivalence shows that $\widehat f$ is its unique morphism to $((Q,t),f)$. On a morphism $k:(X,u)\to(Y,v)$, initiality makes $\Sigma k$ the morphism over the transpose of $\eta_Y k$, namely $Fk$. Thus the universal morphisms define $\Sigma\dashv J$ with unit over $\eta$ and counit over the counit of $F\dashv S$.

Conversely, let $\Sigma\dashv J$ be a lift and write $\Sigma(X,u)=(FX,t)$. Its unit lies over $\eta_X$, so $u\le M_X(t)$. If $u\le M_X(t')$, then $\eta_X$ also defines a morphism $(X,u)\to J(FX,t')$. Its transpose under $\Sigma\dashv J$ is a morphism $(FX,t)\to(FX,t')$ over $1_{FX}$, since $1_{FX}$ is the transpose of $\eta_X$ under $F\dashv S$. Hence $t\le t'$. This proves leastness. $\square$

## 3. Generated theories and inseparability

**Pairs of subobjects.**

Suppose subobjects in $\mathcal C$ admit inverse images. Take $\mathcal H=\operatorname{Sub}^2$, where $\operatorname{Sub}^2(X)=\operatorname{Sub}(X)^2$ is ordered componentwise and $f^*(c,d)=(f^*c,f^*d)$. Let $\mathcal T:\mathcal P^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Preord}$ give the theories of each presentation and their inverse images along translations. Then $\mathsf{Pair}(\mathcal C)=\int\operatorname{Sub}^2$ and $\mathsf{Th}=\int\mathcal T$. Put $\kappa_Q(U)=(U^+,U^-)$, the theorem and refutation subobjects of $SQ$. This defines $\kappa:\mathcal T\Rightarrow\operatorname{Sub}^2\circ S^{\mathrm{op}}$ when extraction is monotone and $(\sigma^*U)^\pm=(S\sigma)^*U^\pm$.

Write $P_X=FX$ and $T_{a,b}=L_X(a,b)$. The lifted adjunction exists exactly when these least theories can be chosen for all triples $(X,a,b)$. For $A=(X,a,b)$, the lemma identifies $((P_X,T_{a,b}),\eta_X)$ as the initial object of $A\downarrow J$. For a target theory $(Q,U)$, every assignment $f:X\to SQ$ extends uniquely to a translation $P_X\to Q$. This translation is a morphism $(P_X,T_{a,b})\to(Q,U)$ precisely when $a\le f^*U^+$ and $b\le f^*U^-$. In logical terms, the theory is freely generated by asserting the generators specified by $a$ and refuting those specified by $b$.

**Restriction to consistent theories.**

Assume that the subobject orders have finite meets, including top, and a pullback-stable bottom. A theory $U$ is **consistent** if $U^+\wedge U^-=\bot$. The adjunction restricts to the full subcategories of consistent theories and of disjoint pairs whose generated theories are consistent. Indeed, if $U$ is consistent, then $(c,d)=(U^+,U^-)$ is disjoint. At $(Q,U)$ the counit gives $T_{c,d}\le\varepsilon_Q^*U$, where $\varepsilon_Q:P_{SQ}\to Q$ extends $1_{SQ}$. Since inverse images preserve disjointness, $\varepsilon_Q^*U$ is consistent. Monotonicity of $\kappa_{P_{SQ}}$ gives consistency of $T_{c,d}$. Thus $J$ and $\Sigma$ take values in the indicated full subcategories, and their hom-set bijection restricts.

For completeness, assume in addition that binary joins exist and inverse images preserve complementary pairs. A theory $U$ is **complete** if $U^+\vee U^-=\top$. A consistent theory is **essentially incomplete** if every consistent extension in its own presentation is incomplete.

For any consistent theory $T$, essential incompleteness is equivalent to the absence of a consistent complete theory receiving a translation from $T$. Indeed, such a target would pull back to a consistent complete extension of $T$. Conversely, any consistent complete extension in the same presentation receives the identity translation.

Now let $a,b$ be disjoint and suppose $T_{a,b}$ is consistent. A **separator** is a complementary pair $c,d$ of subobjects of $X$ with $a\le c$ and $b\le d$. If $(a,b)$ has no separator, there can be no consistent complete target for $T_{a,b}$. An assignment $f$ into such a target would make $f^*U^+,f^*U^-$ a separator.

Every consistent theory receiving a morphism from $(P_X,T_{a,b})$ is essentially incomplete when $(a,b)$ is inseparable, since any consistent complete extension of that theory would again receive a morphism from $(P_X,T_{a,b})$.

For the converse one needs a realization of a separator. Assume that from a separator one can construct a consistent complete theory $U$ and an assignment $f$ satisfying the two signed bounds. Under this additional hypothesis the following are equivalent.

1. The pair $(a,b)$ is inseparable.
2. $T_{a,b}$ is essentially incomplete.
3. No consistent complete theory receives a theory morphism from $(P_X,T_{a,b})$.

The realization hypothesis can fail even when the adjunction exists. Let $S$ forget the distinguished point of a pointed set. The free pointed set on $X$ is $X+\{*\}$. Take as theories on a pointed set all pairs of subsets that omit its distinguished point, ordered by componentwise inclusion. Pointed maps preserve this condition under inverse image. A pair of subsets of $X$, included in the first summand of $X+\{*\}$, is already its least compatible theory. Every disjoint pair $(a,b)$ of subsets of $X$ has the separator $(a,X\setminus a)$, yet no theory is complete, since neither subset contains the distinguished point.

## 4. Propositional and first-order syntax

**Propositional atoms.** Take $\mathcal P$ to be the category of objects of $\mathcal C$ equipped with a unary and a binary operation, with morphisms preserving both. Let $S$ forget the operations. Assume the indicated products and coproducts exist and that $Z\mapsto X+Z+Z^2$ has an initial algebra

$$
[\theta_X,\nu_X,{\Rightarrow}_X]:X+S_X+S_X^2\longrightarrow S_X.
$$

Given an assignment $f:X\to Y$ to an algebra $(Y,n,h)$, initiality applied to $[f,n,h]$ gives the unique morphism $S_X\to Y$ preserving the two operations and extending $f$. Thus $\eta_X=\theta_X$. The structure morphism of the initial algebra is an isomorphism. In the manuscript’s extensive category, the composite of the first coproduct injection with this isomorphism is the monomorphism representing the subobject of **propositional atoms**. This construction requires neither variable names nor decidable equality on $X$.

**Theories on an arbitrary target algebra.** Work in a regular category with disjoint, pullback-stable finite coproducts. On $(Y,n,h)$ write $\neg p=n(p)$ and $p\Rightarrow q=h(p,q)$ in expressions for morphisms. Let $\lambda_Y:Y^2+Y^3+Y^2\to Y$ have components

$$
p\Rightarrow(q\Rightarrow p),\qquad
(p\Rightarrow(q\Rightarrow r))\Rightarrow((p\Rightarrow q)\Rightarrow(p\Rightarrow r)),\qquad
(\neg q\Rightarrow\neg p)\Rightarrow(p\Rightarrow q).
$$

A subobject $U\hookrightarrow Y$ is a theory when $\lambda_Y$ factors through $U$ and $\pi_1^*U\wedge h^*U\le\pi_2^*U$ in $\operatorname{Sub}(Y^2)$. On the free algebra, Appendix A.6 uses the premise $\langle\pi_1,h\rangle$ and conclusion $\pi_2$. The inverse image of $U\times U$ along that premise is $\pi_1^*U\wedge h^*U$, so its binary rule is exactly this inequality. Its nullary rules require the three schemes and the chosen axioms to lie in $U$. If $g:Y\to Z$ preserves the operations, it commutes with each scheme, so $\lambda_Y$ factors through $g^*U$ for each theory $U$ on $Z$. Pulling the modus ponens inequality back along $g\times g$ proves it for $g^*U$. The theorem and refutation subobjects are $U$ and $n_Y^*U$. Since $g n_Y=n_Z g$, one has $n_Y^*g^*U=g^*n_Z^*U$. On the free algebra, the initial derivation algebra of Appendix A.6 gives the least closed theory containing the positive atoms specified by $a$ and the negations specified by $b$. Thus free syntax gives $F\dashv S$, the least closed theory gives $L_X(a,b)$, and preservation of negation gives naturality of $\kappa$. [Appendix A.6](https://github.com/flengyel/CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/blob/d931137fdd8a219bfe896127d2b3587c7ed811c5/manuscript/latex/appendices/a-syntax-and-theories.tex#L596-L623)

**Corollary (propositional inseparability criterion).** Let $\mathcal C$ be a regular category with disjoint, pullback-stable finite coproducts. Fix $X$ for which $Z\mapsto X+Z+Z^2$ has an initial algebra. Let $a,b$ be disjoint subobjects of $X$, and suppose their least generated propositional theory $T_{a,b}$ exists and is consistent. Then $T_{a,b}$ is essentially incomplete if and only if $(a,b)$ is inseparable.

**Proof.** If $U$ were a consistent complete extension, $\theta_X^*U$ and $\theta_X^*\nu_X^*U$ would form a complementary pair containing $a$ and $b$, respectively. Conversely, a complementary pair containing $a,b$, respectively, gives a decomposition $X\cong C+D$. Let $2=1+1$ with injections $\mathbf f,\mathbf t$. Let $d:X\to2$ be true on $C$ and false on $D$. Initiality gives the valuation $v:S_X\to2$ extending $d$ and preserving Boolean negation and implication, by the algebra $[d,\neg_2,{\Rightarrow}_2]:X+2+2^2\to2$. By distributivity, the square and cube of $1+1$ are coproducts of four and eight copies of $1$, respectively. On these summands the Boolean truth tables verify the three schemes and closure under modus ponens, so the true summand is a theory on $2$. Its inverse image $v^*\mathbf t$ is therefore a theory on $S_X$. Its refutation subobject is $v^*\mathbf f$. These two subobjects are complementary, and $v\theta_X=d$ gives the bounds on $a,b$. Thus $v^*\mathbf t$ is a consistent complete extension of $T_{a,b}$. $\square$

**First-order sentences.** Let the base category be regular with disjoint, pullback-stable finite coproducts. Take first-order presentations with the same object $V$ of variable names and let $S$ send a presentation to its sentence object. In the free presentation on $X$, the only nonlogical symbols are nullary predicates. Their formula constructor factors through the sentence object because their free-variable lists are empty. The resulting morphism $\theta_X:X\to S_X$ forms the generating atomic sentences. A translation can send each such atom to an arbitrary target sentence.

Here $V$ has **decidable equality**. Its diagonal is the inverse image of the true injection $1\to 1+1$ under a morphism $V\times V\to 1+1$. The named-variable syntax uses this morphism in computing free-variable lists and admissible substitution. The parameter-stable syntax and list algebras yield the unique extension of an assignment. Initial derivation algebras for axiom subobjects give the generated theories, and inverse images along logical translations preserve closed theories. Writing $i_a,i_b$ for inclusions representing the subobjects of $X$, the least theory $L_X(a,b)$ of §3 is
$\operatorname{Gen}_{P_X}\bigl(\operatorname{im}(\theta_X i_a)\vee\operatorname{im}(\nu_X\theta_X i_b)\bigr)$. [Appendix A.1](https://github.com/flengyel/CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/blob/d931137fdd8a219bfe896127d2b3587c7ed811c5/manuscript/latex/appendices/a-syntax-and-theories.tex#L85-L101) · [Theorem 4.7 and its proof](https://github.com/flengyel/CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/blob/d931137fdd8a219bfe896127d2b3587c7ed811c5/manuscript/latex/sections/03b-internal-adjunctions.tex#L376-L475)

For first-order realization the separator again gives $d:X\to2$. Corollary 4.8 interprets terms in the terminal object, equality by $\mathbf t$ and universal quantification by $\pi_2:V\times2\to2$. The proof verifies substitution and the quantifier and equality axioms before restricting the valuation to sentences. The true and false fibres give the complementary theorem and refutation subobjects required in §3. The comparison theorem then supplies examples of inseparable pairs. [Boolean extension in Corollary 4.8](https://github.com/flengyel/CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/blob/d931137fdd8a219bfe896127d2b3587c7ed811c5/manuscript/latex/sections/03b-internal-adjunctions.tex#L498-L539) · [Diagonal pairs in Corollary 3.3](https://github.com/flengyel/CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/blob/d931137fdd8a219bfe896127d2b3587c7ed811c5/manuscript/latex/sections/03-sections-and-inseparability.tex#L110-L123)

The Lean development proves the assignment criterion for arbitrary pairs of subobjects in the named-variable calculus and the adjunction for consistent theories. [Lean assignment criterion](https://github.com/flengyel/CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/blob/d931137fdd8a219bfe896127d2b3587c7ed811c5/Lean/CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46SignedFirstOrderGeneration.lean#L85-L106) · [Lean adjunction](https://github.com/flengyel/CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/blob/d931137fdd8a219bfe896127d2b3587c7ed811c5/Lean/CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46SignedFirstOrderAdjunction.lean#L24-L91)

## 5. Antecedents

**Universal morphisms and lifted adjunctions.** The comma category $A\downarrow J$ is the category of elements of the covariant functor $B\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_{\int\mathcal H}(A,JB)$. Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, Proposition 2.4.8, characterizes representability of such a functor by an initial object in its category of elements. [Riehl, Proposition 2.4.8](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/context.pdf#page=94)

Hermida’s Theorem 3.2.3 starts with a functor over the base left adjoint $F$ that preserves cartesian morphisms. It characterizes when this functor has a right adjoint in the 2-category of fibrations. In the proof, Hermida obtains the right adjoint over the common base by reindexing along the unit. The same reindexing appears in the formula $M_X=\eta_X^*\kappa_{FX}$ in the notation of §2. Here the given functor is $J$ over $S$, and the lemma constructs its left adjoint $\Sigma$ over $F$. [Hermida, *Fibrations, Logical Predicates and Indeterminates*, Theorem 3.2.3 and proof](https://era.ed.ac.uk/server/api/core/bitstreams/6bbd058b-c2fa-4b08-bcd1-f9dcc8fc27bb/content#page=79)

For $\Sigma$ to preserve cartesian morphisms, $L_X(k^*v)$ and $(Fk)^*L_Y(v)$ must be equivalent for every $k:X\to Y$ and $v\in\mathcal H(Y)$. Applying $\Sigma$ to the cartesian morphism $(X,k^*v)\to(Y,v)$ over $k$ gives $L_X(k^*v)\le (Fk)^*L_Y(v)$. The propositional construction in $\mathbf{Set}$ shows that this inequality can be strict. Let $k:\{x,x'\}\to\{y\}$ send both atoms to $y$, and take $v=(\varnothing,\varnothing)$. Write $x$, $x'$ and $y$ for the corresponding atomic formulas. The first two Hilbert schemes and modus ponens prove $y\Rightarrow y$, so the inverse image of $L_{\{y\}}(v)$ contains $x\Rightarrow x'$. The valuation $x=\mathbf t$, $x'=\mathbf f$ falsifies this formula, so the theory generated by the empty pair on $\{x,x'\}$ omits it. Both theories generated by the empty pair are consistent. A valuation with $x=x'=\mathbf f$ factors through $k$ and satisfies the inverse-image theory, so it too is consistent. Thus $\Sigma$ fails to preserve this cartesian morphism even after restriction to consistent theories.

Section 2 uses the notion of a lifted adjunction in equation (7) of Turkenburg, Beohar, Kupke and Rot. The unit and counit in the total categories lie over the base unit and counit. This definition imposes no cartesian-preservation hypothesis on either functor. The authors cite Winskel’s Lemma 4.5 for preservation of cartesian morphisms by the right adjoint over a fixed base and Hermida’s Lemma 3.3.3(ii) for different bases. Here naturality of $\kappa$ gives this property of $J$ directly. Their Lemma 7, equation (11), gives $L_X\dashv\eta_X^*\kappa_{FX}$ from a lift. Under Assumption 2 the fibres are complete lattices and “reindexing preserves meets.” Lemma 10(2) asks for a left adjoint to $\kappa_Q$ for every $Q$. Section 2 tests the composite $\eta_X^*\kappa_{FX}$ for every $X$ and requires only preorders and monotone reindexing in the fibres. [Turkenburg et al., pp. 6:4, 6:6–8](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CALCO.2023.6) · [Hermida, Lemma 3.3.3](https://era.ed.ac.uk/server/api/core/bitstreams/6bbd058b-c2fa-4b08-bcd1-f9dcc8fc27bb/content#page=83)

**Logical instances.** The theories on arbitrary propositional algebras in §4 are the internal form of deductive filters in logical matrix semantics. Blasio, Caleiro and Marcos close a pair of sets of assertions and denials to obtain its theorems and anti-theorems. Their Lemma 4.1 says that the axiomatization is consistent exactly when these two closed sets are disjoint. In §3 the corresponding condition is $U^+\wedge U^-=\bot$, and in §4 negation determines $U^-=\nu^*U$. [Jansana, *Algebraic Propositional Logic*](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-algebraic-propositional/) · [Blasio, Caleiro and Marcos, §4, Lemma 4.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.02338#page=18)

Voutsadakis’s signature adjunction gives an instance of §1. In $\mathbf{HSet}$ a family $X$ has components $X_N$ for finite sets $N\subset\omega$ of variable names, with $X_N\cap X_M=X_{N\cap M}$. A signature morphism assigns each relation symbol in $X_N$ a target formula whose free variables lie in $N$. Substitution extends the assignment to all formulas. The syntax is first-order without terms. Its atoms are relation symbols and variable equalities, and its constructors are $\neg$, $\wedge$ and $\exists_k$. In Theorem 7 the functor $F:\mathbf{HSet}\to\mathbf{Sign}$ is left adjoint to the formula functor $U$. On p. 485 Voutsadakis identifies $\mathbf{Sign}$ with the Kleisli category of $UF$. Thus the morphisms $FX\to FY$ are exactly the assignments $X\to UFY$ of §1 for this adjunction. A signature carries no chosen theory. The named-variable syntax of §4 uses an internal variable object with decidable equality. [Voutsadakis, Definitions 2–3, p. 478](https://www.voutsadakis.com/RESEARCH/PUBLISHED/fol.pdf#page=6) · [Theorem 7, p. 484](https://www.voutsadakis.com/RESEARCH/PUBLISHED/fol.pdf#page=12) · [Kleisli category, p. 485](https://www.voutsadakis.com/RESEARCH/PUBLISHED/fol.pdf#page=13)

**Inseparability.** Given a nonrecursive computably enumerable (c.e.) set $A$, Shoenfield constructs recursively inseparable c.e. sets $B,C$ of the same Turing degree as $A$ (Theorem 1). In Theorem 2 he axiomatizes a theory $\mathbf T$ of one equivalence relation with at most one class of each finite size. Write $\Phi_n$ for the sentence asserting that some class has exactly $n$ elements. Shoenfield adds $\Phi_n$ for $n\in B$ and $\neg\Phi_n$ for $n\in C$. For positive $n$, models show that $\mathbf T\vdash\Phi_n$ exactly when $n\in B$, and $\mathbf T\vdash\neg\Phi_n$ exactly when $n\in C$. Using Janiczak’s Lemma 2, he reduces each sentence over $\mathbf T$ to a Boolean combination of the $\Phi_n$ and obtains a theory of the degree of $A$. For any consistent extension $V$ of $\mathbf T$, the inverse image $D=\{n\mid V\vdash\Phi_n\}$ of its theorems contains $B$ and misses $C$. If $V$ were decidable, $D$ would be a recursive separator. This proves essential undecidability and gives the inverse-image argument of §3. [Shoenfield, *Degrees of formal systems* (1958), Theorem 1, p. 389, and Theorem 2, pp. 390–391](https://doi.org/10.2307/2964013)

Smullyan, *Theory of Formal Systems* (1961), Chapter III, Theorem 23(b), pp. 59–60, gives the recursive inseparability of the theorem and refutation sets for a consistent theory strongly separating a recursively inseparable pair. Theorem 22, p. 59, obtains recursive inseparability of the provable and refutable sentence codes when every recursive set is definable in a consistent arithmetical theory.

Murwanashyaka, Pakhomov and Visser (MPV), in *There are no minimal essentially undecidable theories*, use the following definition on p. 1161. “A theory is essentially undecidable iff all its consistent extensions in the same language are undecidable.” Decidability concerns a decision procedure for theoremhood. Essential incompleteness in §3 concerns the absence of any consistent complete internal extension in the same presentation.

In §4.1 they call a c.e. theory $T$ **propositional-logic-like** (PLL) if there is a recursive sequence of sentences $(\alpha_i)_{i\in\mathbb N}$ such that its complete consistent extensions are precisely

$$
T_D=T+\{\alpha_i\mid i\in D\}+\{\neg\alpha_i\mid i\notin D\},
\qquad D\subseteq\mathbb N .
$$

This realizes every separator by a completion, as required in §3, and also describes all completions. Remark 4.2 characterizes PLL by a recursive Boolean isomorphism between the numbered Lindenbaum algebra of $T$ and the numbered free Boolean algebra on countably many generators. The corresponding construction in §4 extends an assignment $d:X\to2$ uniquely to a valuation on the free propositional algebra. [MPV, §4.1, pp. 1163–1164](https://research-portal.uu.nl/ws/files/240671111/exad005.pdf#page=6)

MPV take $\mathsf{Jan}$ as their base theory. Besides equivalence and uniqueness of a class of each finite size, its axioms require at least $k$ classes of size at least $k$ for every $k$. In Shoenfield’s signed theory this last schema already follows by choosing $k$ distinct sizes at least $k$ in the infinite set $B$. MPV’s $A_i$ asserts that some class has exactly $i+1$ elements. Their Theorem 4.3 proves that $\mathsf{Jan}$ is PLL. [MPV, Theorem 4.3, p. 1164](https://research-portal.uu.nl/ws/files/240671111/exad005.pdf#page=7)

Given any c.e. set $A$ with index $a$, MPV’s Theorem 4.8 constructs disjoint c.e. sets $B,C$. Part (iii) states that every c.e. separator of $B,C$ computes $A$. Their theory $\mathrm{sh}(a)$ adds $A_i$ for $i\in B$ and $\neg A_i$ for $i\in C$ to $\mathsf{Jan}$. For a consistent c.e. extension $V$, the set $\{i\mid V\vdash A_i\}$ is a c.e. separator computable from $V$. Thus $A\le_T V$. Theorem 4.9 gives $\mathrm{sh}(a)\equiv_T A$ and hence $\mathrm{sh}(a)\le_T V$ for every such $V$. This is Turing persistence. MPV credit both theorems to Shoenfield. [MPV, Theorem 4.8(iii), p. 1166](https://research-portal.uu.nl/ws/files/240671111/exad005.pdf#page=9) · [Theorem 4.9, p. 1167](https://research-portal.uu.nl/ws/files/240671111/exad005.pdf#page=10)

For arbitrary c.e. sets $B,C$ with indices $a,b$, respectively, let $\mathrm{so}(a,b)$ add the same signed axioms to $\mathsf{Jan}$. With $\mathrm{Rsep}$ the set of pairs of indices of recursively separable c.e. sets, MPV’s equivalence in §4.4 is

$$
\langle a,b\rangle\notin\mathrm{Rsep}\quad\text{iff}\quad
\mathrm{so}(a,b)\text{ is essentially undecidable or inconsistent}.
$$

For disjoint $B,C$, independence of the $A_i$ gives consistency. A recursive separator $D$ gives the complete consistent c.e. extension $\mathsf{Jan}_D$, which is decidable by enumerating proofs of a sentence and its negation in parallel. Conversely, a decidable consistent extension $V$ gives the recursive separator $\{i\mid V\vdash A_i\}$. The proof of Theorem 4.6 uses this last implication. Theorem 2.2(i) gives transfer of essential undecidability under interpretation. [MPV, Theorem 2.2(i)](https://research-portal.uu.nl/ws/files/240671111/exad005.pdf#page=5), [Theorem 4.6](https://research-portal.uu.nl/ws/files/240671111/exad005.pdf#page=9) and [§4.4](https://research-portal.uu.nl/ws/files/240671111/exad005.pdf#page=12)

Let $B,C$ be disjoint c.e. sets with indices $a,b$, and let $p,q$ be disjoint subobjects in the setting of §3. Suppose $T_{p,q}$ is consistent and every separator of $(p,q)$ can be realized in a consistent complete theory. If $(p,q)$ has a complementary separator exactly when $(B,C)$ has a recursive separator, then $T_{p,q}$ is internally essentially incomplete exactly when $\mathrm{so}(a,b)$ is essentially undecidable.
